title: The Lesson I Learned From Moses’ Staff
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Moses’ Staff
The Ordinary Thing God Uses to Change Everything
What if the very thing you have overlooked your entire life is the thing God wants to use to change your story?
What if the answer to your prayers is not something you are waiting to receive—but something already sitting in your hand?
That is the lesson I learned from Moses’ staff.
And it changed the way I see my failures, my limitations, my past, and even my purpose.
Because buried inside one simple piece of wood is one of the most powerful messages in all of Scripture.
A message for every person who feels unqualified.
A message for every person who believes God could never use someone like them.
A message for every person carrying a scandal they wish they could erase.
Because from scandal to grace, Jesus rewrites everything.
When most people think about Moses, they imagine the mighty prophet standing before Pharaoh, parting the Red Sea, calling down miracles, and leading an entire nation.
But that is not where Moses’ story begins.
His story begins with failure.
Moses was a man carrying deep regret.
After killing an Egyptian, he fled into the wilderness as a fugitive (Exodus 2:11-15).
The man who would later confront kings spent forty years hiding among sheep.
Forty years.
Not forty days.
Not forty weeks.
Forty years.
Imagine what that does to a person.
Imagine the doubts.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine replaying old mistakes so many times that they become your identity.
Many of us know exactly what that feels like.
Some are hiding behind success.
Others are hiding behind humor.
Some hide in religion.
Others hide in distractions.
But hiding is still hiding.
Then one day everything changed.
Moses encountered God at the burning bush.
And God asked him a question that seems almost strange.
In Exodus 4:2, the Hebrew text says:
"וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו יְהוָה מַה־זֶּה בְיָדֶךָ"
Vayomer elav Yahweh, mah-zeh beyadecha?
"And the LORD said to him, 'What is that in your hand?'"
Moses answered:
Matteh.
"A staff."
Just a staff.
A shepherd's stick.
Nothing impressive.
Nothing expensive.
Nothing powerful.
Just a piece of wood worn smooth by years of ordinary use.
Yet God already knew what was in Moses' hand.
The question was never for God's information.
The question was for Moses' revelation.
Because before God transforms the world through you, He often forces you to see what He has already placed in your hand.
Many people spend their lives praying for what they already possess.
They ask for influence while ignoring opportunities.
They ask for purpose while neglecting gifts.
They ask for miracles while overlooking obedience.
God's question still echoes today.
"What is that in your hand?"
What talent have you buried?
What testimony have you silenced?
What experience have you wasted?
What lesson from your pain could help someone else survive theirs?
What calling have you ignored because it seemed too ordinary?
Moses saw a stick.
God saw a weapon against darkness.
Moses saw a tool for sheep.
God saw an instrument for deliverance.
Moses saw limitations.
God saw possibilities.
Then something remarkable happened.
God instructed Moses to throw the staff to the ground.
The moment he obeyed, it became a serpent.
Then God told him to pick it up again.
And it became a staff once more.
Why?
Because God was teaching Moses a lesson many believers still need today.
The power was never in the staff.
The power was never in Moses.
The power was always in God.
The staff only became extraordinary when surrendered.
And so do we.
One of the greatest deceptions people believe is that God needs extraordinary people.
Scripture repeatedly proves the opposite.
God specializes in using surrendered people.
The world searches for talent.
God searches for availability.
The world celebrates strength.
God works through dependence.
The world admires perfection.
God redeems brokenness.
Throughout Scripture, God consistently chooses unlikely people.
Abraham was old.
Jacob was flawed.
Rahab carried a scandalous past.
David was overlooked.
Peter was impulsive.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Yet God transformed every one of them.
Not because of who they were.
But because of who He is.
Even the Greek language of the New Testament reveals this truth beautifully.
In 2 Corinthians 12:9, Paul records Christ's words:
"Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου"
Arkei soi hē charis mou.
"My grace is sufficient for you."
The word charis means grace, favor, divine empowerment freely given.
Then Jesus says:
"ἡ γὰρ δύναμίς μου ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται"
Hē gar dynamis mou en astheneia teleitai.
"For My power is made perfect in weakness."
Not despite weakness.
In weakness.
Not after weakness.
Through weakness.
That changes everything.
Because many people spend their lives trying to hide their weakness from God.
Meanwhile God wants to use the very thing they are trying to conceal.
The scar you hide may become someone else's healing.
The battle you survived may become someone else's hope.
The testimony you are ashamed of may become someone's proof that God still saves.
Moses' staff eventually became one of the most recognizable objects in biblical history.
With it, plagues confronted Egypt.
The Red Sea opened.
Water flowed from rocks.
A nation witnessed God's power.
But never forget what it was before.
A shepherd's stick.
An ordinary object.
Used by an ordinary man.
Surrendered to an extraordinary God.
That is the lesson.
God rarely starts with what impresses people.
He starts with what people overlook.
Which brings us to Jesus.
Because the story of Moses' staff ultimately points beyond Moses.
Like every great biblical story, it points to Christ.
Moses held a staff.
Jesus carried a cross.
To the world, both looked insignificant.
One was a piece of wood.
The other was an instrument of execution.
Yet God transformed both into symbols of deliverance.
The cross looked like defeat.
It became victory.
It looked like shame.
It became glory.
It looked like scandal.
It became salvation.
Isaiah 53:3 says He was:
"Despised and rejected by men."
The Messiah Himself entered history through what appeared to be weakness.
Yet through His death and resurrection, God accomplished the greatest rescue mission in human history.
This is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
Because it is not merely about bad people becoming good.
It is about dead people being made alive.
It is about sinners becoming sons and daughters.
It is about chains becoming testimonies.
It is about scandal becoming grace.
It is about Jesus rewriting everything.
Maybe today you feel like Moses before the burning bush.
Forgotten.
Disqualified.
Ordinary.
Overlooked.
Maybe you believe your mistakes have permanently damaged your future.
Maybe you think your best years are gone.
Maybe you look at your life and see only a shepherd's staff.
But God sees far more than you see.
He always has.
The God who transformed a fugitive into a deliverer can transform your story too.
The God who used a staff can use your gifts.
The God who redeemed Moses can redeem you.
The God who raised Jesus from the dead still specializes in impossible situations.
So let me ask you the same question God asked Moses.
What is in your hand?
What has God already entrusted to you?
What opportunity have you overlooked?
What calling have you postponed?
What act of obedience have you delayed?
Do not underestimate what God can do with a surrendered life.
One moment of obedience can change generations.
One surrendered gift can reach thousands.
One testimony can lead souls to Christ.
One act of faith can alter eternity.
And if this message challenged, encouraged, or convicted you, do not keep it to yourself.
What is the "staff" God has already placed in your hand?
Your testimony may encourage someone reading these comments who feels ready to give up.
One surrendered thing in God's hands can accomplish more than a lifetime of striving in your own.
